ethics_check.report:
Based on the following text, we would expect an ethics approval statement, and it was present:

> Participants were predominantly in their 30s to 50s (74.6%), and 53.7% were female (Fig. 1c).

> Nearly one in four participants with a normal HbA1c (23.6%) therefore had elevated average glucose.

> Participants were self-selected, fee-paying users of a commercial platform, meal logging was self-reported, and sensor models and interface workflows evolved over time, although associations were consistent across anchor years (Supplementary Table 3).

> Participants paid for platform membership, purchased commercially available CGM sensors, selected which data streams to share, and received no research compensation.

Ethics approval statement:

> This cross-sectional study analyzed a de-identified research export from the Levels digital-health platform, collected between 2022 and 2025 under a decentralized, non-interventional protocol (LH-001) sponsored by Levels Health, Inc. and approved by the Advarra Institutional Review Board (Pro00058897).

power.title: Power Analysis Check
report: No power analyses were detected.

::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

:::

stat_p_nonsig.report: Meta-scientific research has shown nonsignificant p values are commonly misinterpreted. It is incorrect to infer that there is 'no effect', 'no difference', or that groups are 'the same' after p > 0.05. It is possible that there is a true non-zero effect, but that the study did not detect it. Make sure your inference acknowledges that it is possible that there is a non-zero effect. It is correct to include the effect is 'not significantly' different, although this just restates that p > 0.05. Metacheck does not yet analyze automatically whether sentences which include non-significant p-values are correct, but we recommend manually checking the sentences below for possible misinterpreted non-significant p values. ```{r} #| echo: false # table data -------------------------------------- table <- structure(list(Text = c("P = 0.06", "P = 0.06"), Sentence = c("Directly comparing the two discordant groups, participants with elevated average glucose and a normal HbA1c had 19.9% higher fasting insulin (P < 0.001), more frequent hyperinsulinemia (27.5% vs 19.6%), higher HOMA-IR and triglycerides (Supplementary Table 1b), and a trend toward higher hsCRP (27.2% higher; P = 0.06; Fig. 5d,e) than those with an elevated HbA1c and normal average glucose.", "Bars, share with fasting insulin ≥10 µIU/mL (Wilson 95% CI): both normal 12.6% (464 of 3,692); CGM elevated only 27.5% (299 of 1,087); HbA1c elevated only 19.6% (216 of 1,100); both elevated 44.5% (450 of 1,011). e, Fasting insulin was 19.9% higher (95% CI 13.3% to 26.8%; 1,087 vs 1,100 participants) and hsCRP 27.2% higher (95% CI -0.8% to 63.2%; P = 0.06; 228 vs 140; open marker, CI includes 0) in the CGM-elevated-only than in the HbA1c-elevated-only group (ratio of geometric means)." )), row.names = c(NA, -2L), class = c("tbl_df", "tbl", "data.frame" )) # display table ----------------------------------- metacheck::report_table(table, c(0.1, 0.9), 10, FALSE) ``` ::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"} For metascientific articles demonstrating the rate of misinterpretations of non-significant results is high, see: Aczel B, Palfi B, Szollosi A, Kovacs M, Szaszi B, Szecsi P, Zrubka M, Gronau Q, van den Bergh D, Wagenmakers E (2018). “Quantifying Support for the Null Hypothesis in Psychology: An Empirical Investigation.” Advances in Methods and Practices in Psychological Science, 1(3), 357–366. doi:10.1177/2515245918773742. Murphy S, Merz R, Reimann L, Fernández A (2025). “Nonsignificance misinterpreted as an effect’s absence in psychology: Prevalence and temporal analyses.” Royal Society Open Science, 12(3), 242167. doi:10.1098/rsos.242167. For educational material on preventing the misinterpretation of p values, see [Improving Your Statistical Inferences](https://lakens.github.io/statistical_inferences/01-pvalue.html#sec-misconception1). :::

:::

This module runs automated data-quality checks (empty columns, SPSS filter variables, category casing, stray whitespace, numbers stored as text, problematic and colliding column names, mixed text encodings, personal information, spreadsheet formatting, and careless responding) on the extracted data files.
We examined 289 columns across 42 data files.
#### Issues Identified

1 file/column combination has at least one issue.

**About the personal-information flags.** These are pattern matches, not confirmed disclosures, and they are tuned to over-report rather than miss something. Expect false positives:

- **Column names** are matched against identifying words in English and other European languages (`email`, `telefoonnummer`, `geboortedatum`, ...). A column called `phone_number` flags whether or not it holds one, and an empty or already-anonymised column flags on its name alone.
- **Values** are matched against the shape of an identifier. An IP address pattern also matches a version string or a dotted numeric code; a card-number pattern requires both a real issuer prefix and a checksum, but a long numeric ID can still coincide.
- **Free text** is flagged when a column holds long, mostly-distinct prose — the shape open-ended answers take. Most such columns contain no names at all.

A flag means *look at this column*. Where the data is already de-identified (an `ip` column reading `Anonymized`, a `name` column the authors emptied), no action is needed.

```{r} #| echo: false # table data -------------------------------------- table <- structure(list(File = "stable5_cgm_measures.csv", Column = "definition", Issues = "🔒 Personally Identifying Information — Free-text column (median 76 characters, 100% distinct) may contain ..."), row.names = c(NA, -1L), class = "data.frame") # display table ----------------------------------- metacheck::report_table(table, "auto", 20, FALSE) ```
#### Careless Responding
No file could be screened for careless responding.

**What this does not cover.** Only 0 of 42 data files could be screened: the rest had no detectable multi-item scale block, or too few respondents. Even in a screened file, these checks only look at multi-item rating scales — the only place where a repeated or flat answer pattern is interpretable. Single questions, open text, demographics and any item outside a detected scale block are never examined. A respondent can therefore answer most of a survey carelessly and still not be flagged here, and finding nothing is not evidence that a dataset is free of careless responding.

summary_table.ethics_statements: This cross-sectional study analyzed a de-identified research export from the Levels digital-health platform, collected between 2022 and 2025 under a decentralized, non-interventional protocol (LH-001) sponsored by Levels Health, Inc. and approved by the Advarra Institutional Review Board (Pro00058897).
live_data_statements: Participants were predominantly in their 30s to 50s (74.6%), and 53.7% were female (Fig. 1c).
Nearly one in four participants with a normal HbA1c (23.6%) therefore had elevated average glucose.

Participants were self-selected, fee-paying users of a commercial platform, meal logging was self-reported, and sensor models and interface workflows evolved over time, although associations were consistent across anchor years (Supplementary Table 3).
Participants paid for platform membership, purchased commercially available CGM sensors, selected which data streams to share, and received no research compensation.
